Since one batch takes 30 minutes to make 3 pizzas, having the oven fit 2 pizzas at a time takes 15 minutes less time, therefore 30-15=15 minutes. Intuitively, this means that multiplying Camilla's baking rate of 3 pizzas per hour times the 2 pizzas fitting at a time (i.e. 3 pizzas / (30 minutes) / 2 pizzas fit per hour) equals 3 pizzas ~ 6 pizza fit * 1 hour / (30min) = 6/-3 = -2 pizzas in .5 hours. Therefore, -2 pizzas times 1 hour equals -1 hour.

TeX vs NumPyCombat

The NumPycombat solver Defy-3 pointed out that my 1-D solver does only half as many iterations as it should. I spent a bit of time thinking about this and realized that if you have a scoring matrix that someone can see looking at your program you should write it out as a formula without using matrices. It turns out you don't need to brute force this because the German mathematician Max Mertz said  the best way to solve linear equations that are 2 dimensional is to represent them as a matrix.

\[x = \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \\ c\_1 \\ c\_2 \\ \vdots \\ c\_n \end{bmatrix} \]

SSP 3.png
And then evaluate the MVP directly in

\[V = (\text{numpyvec}^2 + \text{partialx}^2)+ (\text{numpyvec}^3 + \text{partialx}^3)+... + (\text{numpyvec}^{n-1} + \text{partialx}^{n-1}) \]

So this means nine steps down the line and then 7 scalar operations to go from x to V because A is 9 times bigger than B, right? Well, if B is a vector that goes one dimension up from x, that is what matters because I can multiply all of those matrices by a scalar.

So all math has to do is put a 3-dimensional vector in down to a 2-dimensional vector and if you are multiplying by a fixed size you can fit it into a smaller block. So if I make J twice bigger the dimensions will become 1 down and 1 up and all that will change is when I move the weights around. However, like 1-layer to 2-layer and 2-layer to 3-layer, jumping dimensions is always doubling the time where dimensions are being shifted around. This is why I end up rewriting most of the code in NumPy.

2. We also know that the total cost was $2 per one half dozen (24).

First, we will need to find out how many crayons you purchased in total.

3. We will calculate the total yards of blue crayons by multiplying the total number of half dozens by the number of half dozen you got:

Now we need to calculate the total cost of all the crayons you bought.

4. We will multiply the total number of crayons (24) by the number of crayons per half dozen (12):

Total Cost = 24 Crayons Per Half Dozen * $2 Crayons Per Half Dozen = $48

Since you bought a dozen (12) colored crayons, the amount you spent is double the cost of just one half dozen, or:

At the store, you spent = 2 X $48 = $96
